# Massed Compute alternative: same NVIDIA GPUs, fixed prices 30% under the market

Massed Compute is an NVIDIA Preferred Partner selling on-demand GPU virtual machines and bare metal from its own Tier III datacenters in the United States (US-East, US-West), aimed at AI training and inference without contracts. Its catalogue runs from single RTX A5000s to 8-GPU B200 and B300 nodes, billed per minute with no setup fees and no bandwidth charges. It also publishes SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA and GDPR compliance, a trust signal most GPU-marketplace competitors do not carry.

results.title: Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud ...
highlights:
Flopper.io started as a specification database: peak TFLOPS by precision, memory, bandwidth and power for every datacenter GPU. Specs answer half of the buying question. The other half is price, and that number lives on 24 different pricing pages, in 24 different units. As of today, the pricing index collects 337 live listings from 24 GPU cloud providers, covering 89 GPUs, normalized to one unit: US dollars per GPU per hour. The pipeline refreshes every six hours and has recorded every price change since 14 July 2026, so each GPU page now carries a price history alongside its spec sheet.

...

The spread is the story. On the day of publication, an on-demand H100 SXM5 80 GB (2022) is listed by 16 providers, and the most expensive listing costs nearly seven times the cheapest. The B200 (2024) shows the same pattern with a three-fold gap across eight clouds. Some of that gap is real: interconnect, storage, support and region all cost money. Some of it is simply price discovery that has not happened yet, because nobody was lining the numbers up.

| GPU | Providers | Cheapest on-demand | Highest on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB | 16 | $1.79/hr | $12.29/hr |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB | 11 | $1.40/hr | $4.10/hr |
| NVIDIA L40S 48 GB | 11 | $0.87/hr | $2.25/hr |
| NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB | 10 | $2.99/hr | $10.60/hr |
| NVIDIA B200 SXM 180 GB | 8 | $4.09/hr | $14.00/hr |
| NVIDIA B300 SXM 288 GB | 6 | $7.40/hr | $11.19/hr |
| AMD Instinct MI300X 192 GB | 5 | $2.39/hr | $6.00/hr |

On-demand, per-GPU, USD, as recorded on 9 September 2026. Spot, community and reserved listings are excluded from the range. Each GPU links to its live pricing page, which will have moved on by the time you read this.

## The 24 Providers

Coverage spans three kinds of seller. Hyperscale and general clouds publish rate cards: Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud, DigitalOcean, OVHcloud, Scaleway and Vultr. AI-first clouds, the neoclouds, sell the dense H100, H200 and Blackwell capacity that training runs need: CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Nebius, Crusoe, DataCrunch, Hyperstack and their peers. Marketplaces, RunPod and Vast.ai, list third-party hosts and set the floor for most consumer and workstation parts.

| Provider | Live listings | GPUs priced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod | 78 | 42 |
| Vast.ai | 70 | 70 |
| Microsoft Azure | 25 | 9 |
| DataCrunch | 23 | 12 |
| CoreWeave | 18 | 10 |
| Hyperstack | 16 | 11 |
| DigitalOcean | 15 | 9 |
| Lambda Labs | 14 | 10 |
| Nebius | 12 | 6 |
| AceCloud | 9 | 9 |
| Paperspace | 8 | 6 |
| Massed Compute | 7 | 7 |
| Oracle Cloud (OCI) | 7 | 7 |
| Together AI | 6 | 3 |
| Crusoe | 6 | 6 |
| Scaleway | 5 | 5 |
| EcoHash | 4 | 1 |
| Cudo Compute | 3 | 3 |
| OVHcloud | 3 | 3 |
| Excess Supply | 2 | 2 |
| Denvr Dataworks | 2 | 1 |
| Vultr | 2 | 2 |
| Latitude.sh | 1 | 1 |
| Beyond.pl | 1 | 1 |

A listing is one GPU at one pricing type from one provider. Vast.ai and RunPod count high because their marketplaces publish hosts for consumer GPUs the dedicated clouds do not carry.

## How the Numbers Are Normalized

No two providers quote the same way. One prices an eight-GPU node, another a single accelerator, a third a monthly contract, and Scaleway prices in euros. Every listing goes through the same four steps before it reaches a page.

- Per GPU, per hour, in USD. Node prices are divided by the GPU count. Monthly rates are divided by 730 hours. Non-USD prices are converted at the live exchange rate on the day of the sync.
- Pricing types are kept apart. On-demand (191 listings), spot or preemptible (31), marketplace community hosts (111) and reserved commitments (4) never share a row. The headline cheapest price on each GPU page is always on-demand, so an interruptible instance cannot masquerade as the market rate.
- Every listing maps to one canonical part. A provider's "H100" is matched to the exact variant it sells, SXM5 or PCIe, 80 GB or 94 GB, so a PCIe price never dilutes the SXM figure. Names the matcher cannot place are logged and dropped rather than guessed.
- Bad data is quarantined, not published. A listing that lands far outside its GPU's price band is held back and flagged for review. Median, dispersion and FP8-per-dollar figures on the pricing index are calculated so that a single bad listing cannot move them.

...

## Price History, Not Just a Snapshot

A price comparison that only shows today cannot tell you whether $2.99 for an H200 is a bargain or the new normal. Since 14 July 2026 the pipeline has recorded 2,297 price points across 58 days and 101 GPUs, appending a row every time a listing changes. Each GPU pricing page plots the last 30 days with one line per provider, so you can see who cut, who held, and who quietly raised.

The index also reports a 30-day change per GPU. That figure compares the same providers' listings at both ends of the window, so a new cloud joining coverage registers as more data, not as a price move.

...

## What It Does Not Cover Yet

Public list prices only. Negotiated enterprise rates, reserved-capacity contracts and volume discounts are not published and are not tracked. Availability is shown where a provider publishes it, and a listed price does not guarantee capacity in the region you need. AWS and Google Cloud are the largest gaps in coverage; both publish pricing in formats that need heavier parsing and validation, and both are next on the list.

Confirm the live rate with the provider before committing. Some outbound links are affiliate links, which fund the pipeline and never change which provider appears cheapest.

results.title: What Does It Really Take to Scale Enterprise AI? - Massed Compute
results.author: Massed Compute
highlights:
One real-world example shared is how a client who was initially convinced that they needed top-tier H100 GPUs actually achieved a better cost-to-performance outcome with NVIDIA’s RTX line, saving millions after benchmarking both options against their actual workload.

## Takeaway 2: GPU Infrastructure, Storage, and Security Decisions Move the Needle

Memory, storage, and networking requirements can shift dramatically depending on whether a workload is training, retraining, or running inference. Benchmarking at multiple points (not just at kickoff) helps teams continually right-size their spend as prices and requirements evolve. 

Compliance and data security are areas that get underestimated. As AI initiatives move faster, sensitive data can end up in the wrong systems if governance isn’t built in from day one.

...

## Takeaway 3: Common Enterprise AI Blindspots Stall Scale Before It Starts

The most valuable part of the discussion centered on what teams wish they had known earlier. For example:

- Underestimating compute costs. GPU and storage prices doubled over the past year, forcing organizations to rethink pricing models and ROI timelines.
- Overlooking data readiness. Teams routinely underestimate the heavy lifting required to organize and connect the data AI systems depend on.
- Over-indexing on one flagship project. It’s best to run small, parallel pilots to build momentum instead of betting everything on a single use case.

Anticipating these blindspots early transforms how your team approaches deployment. By managing compute spend proactively, laying a strong data foundation, and diversifying your pilots, you build a resilient strategy that moves AI out of the lab and delivers measurable, long-term business value.

results.title: Nebius hikes AI cloud prices again as demand for computing power soars | My 95.7
results.author: Thomson Reuters
highlights:
Sept 17 (Reuters) – Cloud provider Nebius said on Thursday it will raise pay-as-you-go prices for leasing selected ​Nvidia chips from October 1, ‌marking the company’s second price hike in three months.

Demand for computing capacity to train and run AI models is surging; rival CoreWeave ‌said ​earlier in the ⁠day that it is ⁠signing contracts at higher prices.

Here are some details:

• Rates for selected Nvidia graphics processing units will rise between ​17% and 21%.

• On-demand rates for some central processing units, made ⁠by AMD and Intel, ⁠and memory offerings have also ​been hiked.

• Prices of some CPU-only instances ​will rise by 25% and those ‌of memory offerings by about 41%, the company said.

• The Amsterdam-based neocloud firm said that customers reserving large-scale clusters ⁠for multiple months can receive commitment discounts.

• Nebius’ price increases follow a quarter of rapid ⁠growth ‌in its AI cloud business, ⁠as the company signed four ​customer ‌contracts averaging more than $1 billion ​each.

results.title: Earning Rate Changes: September 12 - SaladCloud Blog
results.author: Jared Carpenter
highlights:
Salad earning rates change September 12, 2026: RTX 5090 and 4090 rates go up, 15 GPU classes come down at higher priority tiers, CPU payouts rise.

...

GPU prices will change on September 12th, 00:00 UTC. Before you worry, these changes include increased earnings for highly demanded GPUs, and almost all decreases are limited to specific priority tiers. See the chart below if you want to check what your future earning situation will look like. Keep reading for more context as to why we're altering our prices again.

If you're running a 5090 or a 4090, your rates are going up at High, Medium, and Low priority, since demand for those cards keeps outrunning what the network can supply. Fifteen other GPU classes are coming down, mostly at those same three tiers, while Lowest priority stays where it is on everything except the RTX 5080. CPU-only workloads are getting a raise too, covered below. And if your card isn't in the chart at all, nothing about your earnings is changing.

...

For once, some of these changes are increases. Customer demand for the 5090 and 4090 has been outrunning what the network can supply for months now, so on September 12th those two classes get more expensive for customers, and your earning rates on them go up right along with it.

The rest of the changes are decreases across the higher priority tiers. Our lowest priority prices are already highly competitive with the market, so those aren't changing (the RTX 5080 being the one exception), but our higher tiers were overpriced, which discouraged customers from paying more for your GPUs. Needless to say, if our customers can get the same or comparable GPU resources elsewhere, at higher reliability, and cheaper than our higher priority prices, they can and will do so.

While we can't guarantee that this will lead to 100% uptime for everyone who owns the affected GPUs, we expect utilization and priority rates to both increase, leading to more Salad Balance heading into Chefs' pockets.

Payouts for CPU-only workloads are going from $0.0035 to $0.004 per hour per vCPU, which works out to a bit over 14% more for the exact same work.

...

results.title: I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
**Reshared from Prashant Maurya:**
> I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately.
>
> Earlier this year, we were seeing H200s at around $1.80/hour. Today, that same capacity is closer to $2.90 to $3.00/hour.
>
> That is a big jump in a short time.
>
> And even at these prices, people are still trying to find capacity.
> The bigger issue is not just price. It is availability.
>
> November capacity is already heavily booked. Larger December requirements are getting picked up quickly as well. If you are planning a meaningful training run, an inference rollout, or a product launch, leaving compute until the last minute is becoming risky.
>
> I know every team wants lower prices. We all do.
>
> But right now, I would not bet on waiting for capacity to become easier or cheaper. I would start planning earlier and get clarity on what you may need.
>
> At Spheron Network, we have some exclusive H200 and B300 capacity available for October and November.
>
> If you are working through your plans and want to explore options, feel free to reach out.

results.title: The average customer now saves 25% with SFC | SF Compute
results.author: Evan Conrad
highlights:
Today, on-platform customers on SFC receive an average 25% realized discount off their compute price, via resale.

That means a customer buying $100k of compute receives $25k back from selling idle capacity, on average. For a customer who bought at $4.50/GPU/hr, that brings their realized price to $3.375/GPU/hr.
